blocks.html: Before we write a single letter, we get ready. Good writing starts with how you sit.

blocks.name: wr-hand
blocks.cap: A is ready to write. B is bent over the paper.

items: Sit tall, with your back against the chair.
Put both feet flat on the floor.
Rest both arms on the table: one to write, one to hold the paper.

blocks.html: Sit tall, feet flat on the floor, both arms on the table.
When you sit tall, your writing arm has room to move, and you can see the whole line you are writing. The other arm on the table keeps you steady.

blocks.title: What would help?
blocks.q: Ben is writing a story with his face right down by the paper.
steps: His face is too close to the paper.
He can sit up tall and move back a little in his chair.
Now he can see the whole line.
blocks.a: Sit up tall and move back a little.

blocks.html: Kneeling on the chair, curling up sideways or leaning way over the paper. Check three things before you start: back, feet, arms.

For the grown-up. A chair and table at the right height help: feet should reach the floor (a sturdy box or a stack of books works as a footrest). A.N. Palmer’s 1915 course begins the same way; see the site’s Palmer Method guides.

sources.name: A. N. Palmer, The Palmer Method of Business Writing (1915), Lessons 1 to 3: position, posture and pencil hold (public domain; guides on this site)

blocks.html: Now pick up your pencil. The way you hold it helps you make smooth, neat letters.

blocks.name: wr-hand
blocks.cap: The usual way to hold a pencil.

items: Hold the pencil between your thumb and your pointer finger.
Let it rest on your middle finger.
Hold it a little way up from the point, so you can see what you write.
Hold it lightly: no squeezing.

blocks.html: Thumb and pointer finger hold the pencil; the middle finger is its pillow. Hold it a little way up from the point, and lightly.
With the pencil in your fingertips, your fingers can steer it in small curves and lines. A light hold lets the pencil glide instead of digging into the paper.

blocks.name: wr-hand
blocks.cap: Only A holds the pencil the usual way.

blocks.title: Which hold?
blocks.q: Mia holds her pencil with her whole hand wrapped around it.
steps: Her fingers can’t move the pencil, so curves are hard.
She can hold it with her thumb and pointer finger, resting it on her middle finger.
blocks.a: Thumb and pointer finger, resting on the middle finger.

blocks.html: Squeezing the pencil hard, or pinching it right at the sharp point. Try this: hold the pencil, then wiggle the eraser end a little. If you can, your hold is light enough.

For the grown-up. The three-finger hold shown here is the one most teachers show. Some children settle on a four-finger hold and write just as well; if the writing is neat and the hand stays relaxed, there is no need to change it. Left-handed writers use the same hold with the other hand.

sources.name: A. N. Palmer, The Palmer Method of Business Writing (1915), Lessons 1 to 3: position, posture and pencil hold (public domain; guides on this site)

blocks.html: Your paper needs a good spot too. One hand writes, and the other hand holds the paper still.

blocks.name: wr-hand
blocks.cap: A right-handed writer (A) and a left-handed writer (B), each ready to write cursive.

blocks.html: For printing, the paper can sit straight in front of you or tilted a little. For cursive, tilt it more, the same way as your writing arm: the top of the paper leans left if you write with your right hand, and leans right if you write with your left hand.
Keep the paper in front of you and hold it still with your other hand. For cursive, tilt the top toward your other hand.
A sliding paper makes wobbly lines. Tilting it lets your arm move along the line easily and keeps your writing hand from covering the words you just wrote.

blocks.title: Which way?
blocks.q: Leo writes with his left hand. He is starting cursive.
steps: Leo’s writing hand is his left hand.
So the top of his paper leans to the right.
His right hand holds the paper still.
blocks.a: Top of the paper to the right; right hand holds it.

blocks.html: Copying the tilt of a friend who writes with the other hand. Your tilt follows your own writing hand.

For the grown-up. A strip of tape on the table can mark the paper’s angle so it is the same each day. Palmer’s course gives the same advice for left-handed writers: mirror the directions and tilt the paper the other way.

sources.name: A. N. Palmer, The Palmer Method of Business Writing (1915), Lessons 1 to 3: position, posture and pencil hold (public domain; guides on this site)

blocks.html: Writing paper has lines that tell each letter how tall to be. There is a top line, a dotted middle line, and the baseline at the bottom, where every letter sits.

blocks.name: wr-letter
blocks.cap: h is tall, a is short, and g has a tail.

head: Kind
Where it goes
Letters
rows: from the baseline up to the top line
b d f h k l t (and every capital)
from the baseline up to the middle line
a c e i m n o r s u v w x z

blocks.html: Every letter sits on the baseline. Short letters reach the middle line, tall letters reach the top line, and tail letters dip below the baseline.
When letters are the right size, a reader can tell them apart at a glance: a tall h is not a short n, and a g with a tail is not an a.

blocks.title: What kind of letter?
blocks.q: Look at y.
steps: It starts at the middle line.
Its long slant goes down below the baseline.
blocks.a: y is a tail letter.

blocks.name: wr-sort

cards.why: j starts at the middle line and its tail goes below.

blocks.cap: Sort the letters by size.

blocks.html: Letting letters float above the baseline, or making the tail of g and y stop on the baseline. Run your finger along the baseline: every letter should touch it.
For the grown-up. The site’s Practice sheets page prints handwriting paper with these three lines in large, medium and small sizes, and can put gray letters on it to trace.

sources.name: Common Core State Standards, English Language Arts, Kindergarten, Language standard L.K.1a: print many upper- and lowercase letters (California Department of Education)
A. N. Palmer, The Palmer Method of Business Writing (1915), Lessons 1 to 3: position, posture and pencil hold (public domain; guides on this site)

blocks.html: Every print letter is made of just a few kinds of strokes: lines down, lines across, slants and circles. A stroke is one move of the pencil, from the time it touches the paper until it lifts.

blocks.name: wr-letter
blocks.cap: t takes two strokes: a line down, then a line across. Press “Show me how” to watch again.

blocks.html: Each letter has its strokes in an order, and each stroke has a start and a direction. The green 1 shows where to begin.
When you make each letter the same way every time, your hand learns it, and writing gets faster and neater. Starting in the same place also keeps letters the same size.

blocks.title: Count the strokes
blocks.q: How many strokes make capital E?
steps: A line down.
A line across the top.
A line across the middle.
A line across the bottom.
blocks.a: Four strokes.

blocks.name: wr-trace
blocks.cap: Trace l with your finger, a mouse or a pen. Start at the green dot.

blocks.html: Drawing a letter like a picture, starting anywhere and going any way. Look for the green 1 and the arrows, and make the strokes in that order.

For the grown-up. Tracing on the screen is a warm-up; real paper and pencil come next. Print a page from Practice sheets with gray letters to trace. Short, frequent practice (five or ten minutes) works better than long sessions.

sources.name: Common Core State Standards, English Language Arts, Kindergarten, Language standard L.K.1a: print many upper- and lowercase letters (California Department of Education)

blocks.html: Here is a rule that helps with almost every letter: start at the top. Lines are pulled down, not pushed up.

Tall letters like b, h, k, l and t start at the top line. Most short letters start at the middle line. The c letters (a, c, d, g, o, q) start just below the middle line and curve back around, the way c does.

blocks.name: wr-letter
blocks.cap: h starts at the top line, n at the middle line, c just below the middle line.

blocks.html: Start at the top: tall letters at the top line, short letters at the middle line, c letters just under the middle line.
Pulling the pencil down toward you is easier to control than pushing it up, and starting from the top keeps your letters lined up across the page.

blocks.title: Where does it start?
blocks.q: Where does the first stroke of d start?
steps: d is tall, but it begins with a c.
So its first stroke starts just below the middle line and curves around.
Then the second stroke starts at the top line and comes straight down.
blocks.a: Just below the middle line (the c), then the top line for the tall line.

blocks.html: Starting a line at the bottom and pushing up, or starting a tall letter at the middle line, so it comes out short. Find the green 1 before you write.
For the grown-up. Saying the strokes aloud helps: “b: start at the top, pull down, back up, around.” Next comes Stick Letters.

sources.name: Common Core State Standards, English Language Arts, Kindergarten, Language standard L.K.1a: print many upper- and lowercase letters (California Department of Education)

blocks.html: Now we write real letters! The first three are made of straight lines only: l, i and t. Remember from Start at the Top: lines are pulled down.

blocks.name: wr-letter
blocks.cap: Press “Show me how” to watch l, i and t.

items: l: start at the top line and pull straight down to the baseline.
i: start at the middle line and pull down to the baseline. Then lift and make a dot above it.
t: start at the top line and pull down. Then cross it on the middle line, left to right.

blocks.html: l is tall, i is short with a dot, and t is tall with a cross on the middle line.
The height tells a reader which letter it is. A short i next to a tall l looks different at a glance, and the cross on the middle line keeps t from looking like a plus sign.

blocks.title: Write the word it
blocks.q: How do you write the word it?
steps: i: start at the middle line, pull down, then make the dot.
Leave a little space.
t: start at the top line and pull down to the baseline.
Cross the t on the middle line.
blocks.a: i (down, dot), then t (down, cross).

blocks.name: wr-trace
blocks.cap: Trace t: the line down first, then the cross.

blocks.html: Making i as tall as l, or crossing t at the top line so it looks like a capital T. Check: does i stop at the middle line? Is the cross of t on the middle line?
For the grown-up. Say the strokes together as your child writes: “Top line, pull down. Middle line, across.” Print a row of each letter from the Practice sheets page to trace and then copy.

sources.name: Common Core State Standards, English Language Arts, Kindergarten, Language standard L.K.1a: print many upper- and lowercase letters (California Department of Education)

blocks.html: Six letters start the same way as c: c, o, a, d, g and q. Start just below the middle line, on the right side, and curve back toward the left, down and around.

blocks.name: wr-letter
blocks.cap: Every one begins with the c curve. Press “Show me how.”

blocks.html: For c, stop at the bottom. For o, keep going and close the circle. For a, d, g and q, close the circle, then add a line down on the right: short for a, tall for d (it starts at the top line), and a tail for g and q.
Circle letters start like c: just below the middle line, curving back to the left and around.
When every circle goes the same way, the line down meets the circle right where the pencil ends up, so a, d, g and q come out neat and closed.

blocks.title: Write a
blocks.q: How do you write a?
steps: Start just below the middle line, on the right.
Curve back to the left, down to the baseline and up around to close the circle.
Lift, and pull a short line down on the right side, from the middle line to the baseline.
blocks.a: A c-curve closed into a circle, then a line down.

blocks.name: wr-trace
blocks.cap: Trace a. Start at the green dot.

blocks.html: Starting the circle at the bottom, or going around the other way (like a clock’s hands). Then the line down doesn’t meet the circle. Check that the curve starts by going left, like c.
For the grown-up. If your child draws circles the other way, trace a large c in the air together, then on paper. The d in b, d, p and q depends on this habit.

sources.name: Common Core State Standards, English Language Arts, Kindergarten, Language standard L.K.1a: print many upper- and lowercase letters (California Department of Education)

blocks.html: These letters have a line down and then a hump: r, n, m, h, and b and p with a round bump. They all begin with a line pulled down, as in Start at the Top.

blocks.name: wr-letter
blocks.cap: The 2 shows where the hump begins: on the line you just made.

items: n: pull down from the middle line. Go back up the line, then over the hump and down.
r: like n, but stop just after the top of the hump.
m: like n with a second hump the same size.
h: a tall line from the top line, then the hump of n.
b and p: a line down (tall for b, a tail for p), then back up and around into a round bump.

blocks.html: Line down first, then back up the line and over: the hump always starts on the line.
When the hump grows out of the line, the letter holds together. A hump that starts away from the line leaves a gap, and n can look like r and a little line.

blocks.title: n or h?
blocks.q: What is the only difference between n and h?
steps: Both have a line down and a hump.
n’s line starts at the middle line.
h’s line starts at the top line.
blocks.a: h has a tall line; n has a short one.

blocks.name: wr-trace
blocks.cap: Trace n: down, then the hump.

blocks.html: Starting the hump away from the line, or making the second hump of m smaller or bigger than the first. Check: both humps of m should reach the middle line and come down to the baseline.

For the grown-up. Some children slide back up the line without lifting the pencil; others lift and start the hump on the line, as the numbered picture shows. Both make a good n. What matters is that the hump starts on the line.

sources.name: Common Core State Standards, English Language Arts, Kindergarten, Language standard L.K.1a: print many upper- and lowercase letters (California Department of Education)

blocks.html: Slant letters lean. Their lines go down to the right, down to the left, or both: v, w, x, y, z and k.

blocks.name: wr-letter
blocks.cap: Watch where each slant starts and which way it goes.

items: v: slant down to the baseline, then slant back up. w does it twice.
x: slant down to the right, lift, then slant down to the left. The lines cross in the middle.
y: a short slant down to the baseline, then a long slant from the right side all the way below the baseline.
z: across, slant down to the left, across again.
k: a tall line, then a slant in and a slant out.

blocks.html: Slants start at the top of the letter and lean the same amount on both sides.
Even slants make v and w look balanced, and the long slant of y is what tells a reader it is y and not v.

blocks.title: Write y
blocks.q: Which slant of y goes below the baseline?
steps: The first slant starts on the left at the middle line and stops at the baseline.
The second starts on the right at the middle line.
It crosses the first one at the baseline and keeps going down below it.
blocks.a: The second, long slant from the right.

blocks.name: wr-trace
blocks.cap: Trace x: two slants that cross.

blocks.html: Making one side of v or w longer than the other, or starting y’s long slant on the left, which makes a backward y. Check: the long slant of y always starts on the right.
For the grown-up. Left-handed writers make the same strokes in the same order; some find it easier to pull the second slant of x toward themselves. Either way, the letter should look the same.

sources.name: Common Core State Standards, English Language Arts, Kindergarten, Language standard L.K.1a: print many upper- and lowercase letters (California Department of Education)

blocks.html: Five letters have moves of their own: e, f, j, s and u. You already know the c curve from Circle Letters and the line down and up from Down, Up and Over.

blocks.name: wr-letter
blocks.cap: Find the green 1 on each letter.

head: Letter
How it goes
rows: Start in the middle of the short space with a line across to the right, then curve up, back and around like c.
Start near the top line with a little hook, curve over and pull down. Then cross it on the middle line.
Start at the middle line, pull down below the baseline and curl left. Then the dot.
Start just below the middle line on the right. Curve back, then forward, then back: a snake.
Pull down from the middle line, curve around the bottom and up. Then a line down on the right.

blocks.html: e starts with a line across, not at the top; s starts on the right and curves back first.
Starting e with its line makes the little closed space at its top. Starting s on the right makes it face the right way every time.

blocks.title: Where does e start?
blocks.q: Ruby starts e at the top, like c. What happens?
steps: The curve comes around first.
Then the line has to be added inside, and it often misses.
Start with the line across the middle, then curve up and around.
blocks.a: Start with the line across, then curve.

blocks.name: wr-trace
blocks.cap: Trace s, starting on the right.

blocks.html: Making s backward, or starting e at the top. Check s: its top curve opens to the right, like a c.
For the grown-up. Backward s is common for a while and fades with practice. Point to the top curve and say, “Starts like c.”

sources.name: Common Core State Standards, English Language Arts, Kindergarten, Language standard L.K.1a: print many upper- and lowercase letters (California Department of Education)

blocks.html: You know all 26 small letters now. Each one has a size, from The Lines We Write On: tall, short or with a tail.

blocks.name: wr-join
blocks.cap: h is tall; a and o are short; p, y and g have tails.

head: Kind
Letters
Where they go
rows: b d f h k l t
a c e i m n o r s u v w x z

blocks.html: Tall letters touch the top line, short letters stop at the middle line, and tails hang below the baseline.
Readers know words partly by their shapes: the ups and downs. When sizes are right, a word like happy is easy to read even from across the room.

blocks.title: Sort the word
blocks.q: Which letters in jump are tall, short and tail letters?
steps: j has a tail.
u and m are short.
p has a tail.
No letter in jump is tall.
blocks.a: Tails: j and p. Short: u and m.

blocks.name: wr-sort

cards.why: t is tall: it starts at the top line.

blocks.cap: Sort the letters.

blocks.html: Letting tails sit on the baseline, so g looks like a and y looks like v. Check each tail letter: does it hang below the line?
For the grown-up. On lined paper, have your child color the space between the baseline and middle line lightly. Short letters live in the colored band.

sources.name: Common Core State Standards, English Language Arts, Kindergarten, Language standard L.K.1a: print many upper- and lowercase letters (California Department of Education)

blocks.html: Capital letters are big. Every capital starts at the top line and reaches the baseline. We begin with the six made of straight lines only: E, F, H, I, L and T.

blocks.name: wr-letter
blocks.cap: Lines down first, then lines across, top to bottom.

items: Make the line down first.
Then the lines across, from the top down, each one going left to right.
E and F have a middle bar on the middle line. E has a bottom bar; F doesn’t.

blocks.html: Down first, then across from top to bottom, each line left to right.
The same order every time lets your hand learn the letter. Going top to bottom means your hand never covers what you still have to line up.

blocks.title: Write E
blocks.q: In what order do the four lines of E go?
steps: 1: a line down from the top line to the baseline.
2: across the top.
3: across the middle line (a little shorter).
4: across the bottom.
blocks.a: Down, then top, middle, bottom.

blocks.name: wr-trace
blocks.cap: Trace E, line by line.

blocks.html: Putting the middle bar of E or F too high or too low. Check: it sits on the dotted middle line.
For the grown-up. Capitals come at the start of names and sentences. Writing your child’s own name is a good first capital practice. See Start at the Top for why lines go down.

sources.name: Common Core State Standards, English Language Arts, Kindergarten, Language standard L.K.1a: print many upper- and lowercase letters (California Department of Education)

blocks.html: Nine capitals use slanted lines: A, K, M, N, V, W, X, Y and Z. Like every capital from Capitals with Straight Lines, they go from the top line to the baseline.

blocks.name: wr-letter
blocks.cap: A: two slants, then the bar. N: down, slant, down. Z: across, slant, across.

items: A: from the top, slant down left; from the top again, slant down right; then the bar across.
M and N: a line down, then slants. The middle of M goes all the way down to the baseline.
V and W: slant down and back up.
Z: across the top, slant down to the left, across the bottom.

blocks.html: Slant capitals start at the top line, and their slants reach all the way to the baseline.
N and Z have a direction. When N slants down to the right and Z slants down to the left, everyone reads them the same way.

blocks.title: Which way does N go?
blocks.q: After the first line down, where does the slant of N go?
steps: Go back to the top of the first line.
Slant down to the right, to the baseline.
Then a line down on the right side, from the top line.
blocks.a: Down to the right.

blocks.name: wr-trace
blocks.cap: Trace N.

blocks.html: Writing N or Z backward, or stopping the middle of M halfway up. Check N: the slant goes down to the right, like sliding down a slide from the left.
For the grown-up. Backward N and Z are common in kindergarten and fade with practice. The Practice sheets page can print capitals to trace.

sources.name: Common Core State Standards, English Language Arts, Kindergarten, Language standard L.K.1a: print many upper- and lowercase letters (California Department of Education)

blocks.html: The last capitals use curves: B, C, D, G, J, O, P, Q, R, S and U. Some start with a line down, and some start with a curve.

blocks.name: wr-letter
blocks.cap: B and D start with a line down. C and O start with a curve near the top.

head: Starts with
Letters
Then
rows: back to the top and curve around to the right
curve back to the left, like a big c
J hooks left at the bottom; U curves up the other side

blocks.html: B, D, P and R start with a line down. C, G, O, Q and S start near the top and curve back to the left.
B has two bumps and D has one big one. Making the line first gives both bumps of B a place to start, so they come out the right size.

blocks.title: Write B
blocks.q: How is B made?
steps: A line down from the top line.
From the top, a bump that ends at the middle line.
From the middle, a second bump down to the baseline.
blocks.a: Line, top bump, bottom bump.

blocks.name: wr-trace
blocks.cap: Trace C, starting near the top.

blocks.html: Making the two bumps of B into one big bump (that makes D), or starting C at the bottom. Check: B’s bumps meet at the middle line.
For the grown-up. Q is O with a short tail across its bottom right. Next come the letters that are easiest to flip: b, d, p and q.

sources.name: Common Core State Standards, English Language Arts, Kindergarten, Language standard L.K.1a: print many upper- and lowercase letters (California Department of Education)

blocks.html: b and d are mirror images, and so are p and q. They are the letters children flip most. A simple rule helps: d begins with c, and c comes before d in the alphabet.

blocks.name: wr-letter
blocks.cap: b and p start with a line. d and q start with a c curve.

head: Letter
First stroke
Then
rows: back up and around into the bump
a tall line down on the right
a line down below the baseline
back up and around into the bump
a line down below the baseline

blocks.html: b and p: line first. d and q: c first.
When you always start the same way, the letter can’t come out backward. The capital B also starts with a line, from Capitals with Curves.

blocks.title: Write dad
blocks.q: How do you start each d in dad?
steps: d: start with c, close it, then the tall line down.
a: start with c, close it, then a short line down.
d: c again, then the tall line.
blocks.a: Every letter in dad starts with c.

blocks.name: wr-sort
blocks.cap: Sort the letters by their first stroke.

blocks.html: Writing b for d (or p for q). Check by asking: did this letter start with a line or with c?
For the grown-up. Flipping b and d is very common in young writers and usually fades with practice. Saying “d begins with c” while writing helps more than correcting finished words.

sources.name: Common Core State Standards, English Language Arts, Kindergarten, Language standard L.K.1a: print many upper- and lowercase letters (California Department of Education)

blocks.html: Letters in a word are like friends holding hands: close together, but not on top of each other.

blocks.name: wr-join
blocks.cap: A is one word. In B, the big gap makes it look like two words.

blocks.html: Inside a word, letters sit close, with just a little space between them.
Readers use spaces to find where words begin and end. A big gap inside a word tells the reader “new word here,” so ju mp looks like two words.

blocks.title: Check a word
blocks.q: Omar wrote c at for cat. What should he change?
steps: There is a big gap between c and a.
That makes it look like two words: c and at.
He can write the letters closer: cat.
blocks.a: Move the letters closer together.

items: Finish a letter, then start the next one just a little way over.
Round letters (o, c, a) can sit a bit closer than straight ones.
Letters should not touch or bump into each other.

blocks.html: Leaving big gaps inside a word, or squeezing letters until they touch. Check by reading your word out loud: does it look like one word?
For the grown-up. Spacing comes with practice and with letters that are the right size (Tall, Short and Tail Letters). Praise the words that look right rather than pointing out every gap.

sources.name: Common Core State Standards, English Language Arts, Kindergarten, Language standard L.K.1a: print many upper- and lowercase letters (California Department of Education)

blocks.html: Between words we leave a bigger space: about the width of one finger. Many children put a finger down after each word, then start the next word on the other side of it.

blocks.name: wr-join
blocks.cap: A has finger spaces. B runs the words together.

blocks.html: Leave a finger space between words, and after a period before the next sentence.
Spaces tell the reader where one word ends and the next begins. Without them, Iseeafrog is a puzzle; with them, I see a frog is easy.

blocks.title: Two sentences
blocks.q: Where do spaces go in: We ran.It was fun.
steps: Between We and ran.
After the period, before It.
Between It, was and fun.
blocks.a: We ran. It was fun.

blocks.html: Forgetting the space after a period. A new sentence is a new word too, so it needs its finger space.
For the grown-up. A craft stick or a clothespin makes a good “spaceman” for children who find finger spaces awkward. Left-handed writers can use a finger of the other hand, or the stick.

sources.name: Common Core State Standards, English Language Arts, Kindergarten, Language standard L.K.1a: print many upper- and lowercase letters (California Department of Education)

blocks.html: Neat writing sits on the baseline, the way books sit on a shelf. Each letter also stays its own size: tall, short or tail, as in Tall, Short and Tail Letters.

blocks.name: wr-join
blocks.cap: In B, one letter floats above the baseline. Can you find it?

blocks.html: Every letter touches the baseline, and only tails go below it.
When letters sit on one line, the eye can slide along the line smoothly. A floating or giant letter makes a reader stop and look twice.

blocks.title: Find the problem
blocks.q: In Ava’s line, each word is a little bigger than the one before. What can she do?
steps: Look at the lines: short letters should stop at the middle line every time.
Her letters grow past it near the end.
She can slow down and check the middle line as she goes.
blocks.a: Keep short letters at the middle line all the way across.

blocks.html: Letters drifting up at the end of a line, or growing bigger as you go. Check: run your finger along the baseline. Every letter should touch it.
For the grown-up. Wide-ruled paper with a dotted middle line helps most at this stage; the Practice sheets page prints it in three sizes.

sources.name: Common Core State Standards, English Language Arts, Kindergarten, Language standard L.K.1a: print many upper- and lowercase letters (California Department of Education)

blocks.html: Copying a sentence neatly uses everything you have learned. Copy one word at a time, then check your copy against the model.

blocks.name: wr-join
blocks.cap: A model sentence to copy.

items: Read the whole sentence first.
Look at one word, then write it.
Leave a finger space and go on to the next word.
At the end, read your copy and the model side by side.

blocks.html: Check four things: a capital at the start, every word there, finger spaces, and the end mark.
Copying fast makes it easy to skip a word or a letter. Checking word by word catches it, and that habit helps every time you write.

blocks.title: Check a copy
blocks.q: Model: My cat can jump. Copy: My cat jump.
steps: Read the copy word by word against the model.
My, cat … the model says can next, but the copy says jump.
The word can is missing.
blocks.a: The word can was skipped.

opts.title: Check my copy
items: A capital letter at the start
Every word is there
Letters sit on the baseline
A finger space between words
A mark at the end

blocks.html: Copying quickly and skipping a word. Point to each word in the model and in your copy, one at a time.
For the grown-up. Keep copy work short: one sentence done carefully beats a page done fast. The checklist above prints with the button below it.

sources.name: Common Core State Standards, English Language Arts, Kindergarten, Language standard L.K.1a: print many upper- and lowercase letters (California Department of Education)

blocks.html: Numbers are written from the top too. Every number is as tall as a capital: from the top line to the baseline.

blocks.name: wr-letter
blocks.cap: Press “Show me how” to watch 0, 1, 2, 3 and 4.

head: Number
How it goes
rows: Start at the top, curve down to the left, around the bottom and up to close.
Start at the top line and pull straight down.
Start near the top on the left, curve up and around to the right, slant down to the bottom left, then go across.
Start near the top on the left, curve around to the middle, then around again to the bottom.
Slant down from the top and go across. Lift, then a line down from the top line.

blocks.html: Numbers start at the top: 0 curves left first, and 2 and 3 curve to the right.
People need to read numbers exactly: in a phone number or a math answer, a 4 that looks like a 9 is a different number.

blocks.title: Write 4
blocks.q: How many strokes make 4, and which comes first?
steps: Stroke 1: slant down from the top, then straight across.
Lift the pencil.
Stroke 2: a line down from the top line, crossing the first stroke.
blocks.a: Two strokes; the slant and across come first.

blocks.name: wr-trace
blocks.cap: Trace 2.

blocks.html: Starting 0 at the bottom, or writing 3 backward. Check 3: both of its curves bulge to the right.
For the grown-up. Writing numbers 0 to 20 is a kindergarten math goal in the Common Core. Writing the numbers on a calendar or a page of math is good practice.

sources.name: Common Core State Standards, Mathematics, Kindergarten, K.CC.3: write numbers from 0 to 20 (California Department of Education)
Common Core State Standards, English Language Arts, Kindergarten, Language standard L.K.1a: print many upper- and lowercase letters (California Department of Education)

blocks.html: Now 5, 6, 7, 8 and 9, written from the top, as in Writing 0, 1, 2, 3 and 4.

blocks.name: wr-letter
blocks.cap: Watch where each number begins.

head: Number
How it goes
rows: Pull down a little from the top line, then around the round belly. Lift, and put on its hat: a line across the top.
Start near the top on the right, curve down to the left all the way to the bottom, and around into a loop.
Across the top, then slant down to the left.
Start near the top on the right, curve left and down like an S, then come back up to close.
A small circle at the top, then a line down on its right side.

blocks.html: 5 gets its hat last; 8 is one stroke, an S that comes back up.
Making the body of 5 first keeps it in one smooth motion; the hat is easy to add after. One stroke for 8 keeps its two loops touching in the middle.

blocks.title: Write 5
blocks.q: Leo put the hat on 5 first and then lost his place. What order works better?
steps: Start at the top line and pull down a little.
Curve around the belly to the bottom.
Lift, go back to the top, and draw the hat across.
blocks.a: Down and around first; the hat last.

blocks.name: wr-trace
blocks.cap: Trace 8 in one stroke.

blocks.html: Drawing 8 as two circles stacked up. It is faster and neater as one stroke: an S, then back up.
For the grown-up. Some families and schools teach 5 or 8 a little differently; if your child’s numbers are clear and start at the top, that’s fine.

sources.name: Common Core State Standards, Mathematics, Kindergarten, K.CC.3: write numbers from 0 to 20 (California Department of Education)

blocks.html: Some numbers face a certain way, and it is easy to write them backward: 2, 3, 5, 7 and 9. Almost every child does it sometimes. Here is how to check.

blocks.name: wr-join
blocks.cap: A is the right way. B is backward.

items: 3 and 5: their round parts bulge to the right.
2 and 7: the top goes across to the right, then slants back down to the left.
9: the circle is on the left, the line on the right.

blocks.html: Curves of 2, 3 and 5 bulge to the right; 9 has its circle on the left.
A backward number can still be read, but it slows the reader down, and in math it can be mistaken for a different number.

blocks.title: Fix it
blocks.q: Hana wrote 9 with the circle on the right. What should she do?
steps: A 9 has its circle on the left.
Start the circle at the top and go left, around, and back up.
Then pull the line down on the right side of the circle.
blocks.a: Circle on the left, line on the right.

blocks.html: Writing 3, 5, 7 or 9 backward. Look at a number line or a clock and compare.
For the grown-up. Reversed numbers are common at first and usually fade with practice. Starting each number at its green dot (Writing 5 to 9) prevents most flips.

sources.name: Common Core State Standards, Mathematics, Kindergarten, K.CC.3: write numbers from 0 to 20 (California Department of Education)

blocks.html: You can print neatly now (Copying Neatly). Next comes cursive, a way of writing where the letters of a word are joined, so the pencil stays on the paper until the word is done.

blocks.name: wr-join
blocks.cap: The same word in print (A) and in cursive (B).

blocks.html: Cursive uses the same 26 letters as print, with joining strokes and some new shapes.
Because the pencil doesn’t lift between letters, cursive can be quick and smooth. People also use it to sign their names, and knowing it lets you read old letters and documents.

blocks.title: Same or different?
blocks.q: Is cursive a new alphabet?
steps: Cursive has the same letters: a, b, c and on to z.
Each letter has a little stroke that leads in and one that leads out.
Some letters look a lot like print (a, d, o), and some look new (r, s, f).
blocks.a: No: the same letters, joined.

blocks.name: wr-join
blocks.cap: The joining strokes are colored. Open dots show where a letter ends; filled dots show where the next one begins.

blocks.html: Thinking cursive is a different set of letters to memorize from scratch. Look for the print letter inside each cursive one.

For the grown-up. The cursive taught here is a traditional American style in the manner of A. N. Palmer’s 1915 course, which the site guides lesson by lesson (Palmer Method guides). Paper tilt matters more for cursive: see Placing the Paper.

sources.name: Grokipedia, “Cursive”
A. N. Palmer, The Palmer Method of Business Writing (1915), Lessons 1 to 3: position, posture and pencil hold (public domain; guides on this site)

blocks.html: Most cursive letters are built from four strokes. Learn these, and the letters come easily.

blocks.name: hand-strokes
blocks.cap: The four basic strokes. The green dot is where the pencil starts.

head: Stroke
Looks like
Begins the letters
rows: a swing up, like a smile
i t u w e l
n m v x y z
the start of c, curving back and down
a c d g o q

blocks.html: Inside a word, the stroke that joins two letters is often one of these curves too: an undercurve into i, an overcurve into n.
Undercurve, overcurve, downcurve and slant line: four strokes that build the cursive alphabet.
Curves join smoothly; corners don’t. When the curves really curve, one letter flows into the next.

blocks.title: Find the strokes in i
blocks.q: Which strokes make cursive i?
steps: An undercurve swings up from the baseline to the middle line.
A slant line comes down to the baseline.
Another undercurve swings up and out. Then the dot.
blocks.a: Undercurve, slant line, undercurve, dot.

blocks.name: wr-trace
blocks.cap: Trace cursive i and feel the undercurve.

blocks.html: Making the curves into straight lines with sharp corners. Then letters are hard to join. Let the pencil swing.
For the grown-up. Palmer began with large ovals and push-pull drills to loosen the arm; the site’s Palmer drill guides show them. A few minutes of curves before letters is a good warm-up.

sources.name: A. N. Palmer, The Palmer Method of Business Writing (1915), Lessons 1 to 3: position, posture and pencil hold (public domain; guides on this site)
Grokipedia, “Cursive”

blocks.html: Cursive letters lean, like rain blowing in the wind. The important thing is that they all lean the same way.

blocks.name: hand-slant
blocks.cap: In A every letter leans the same way. In B the second t stands straight up.

blocks.html: Every letter leans the same amount, in the same direction.
Even slant makes cursive look calm and easy to read. When letters lean different ways, the word looks wobbly and letters can be misread.

blocks.title: What helps the slant?
blocks.q: Sam’s letters lean every which way. What can he try?
steps: Tilt the paper the right way for his writing hand.
Pull each slant line down toward himself, the same way each time.
Then all the letters lean together.
blocks.a: Tilt the paper and pull every slant the same way.

blocks.name: wr-hand
blocks.cap: Tilt for a right hand (A) and for a left hand (B).

blocks.html: Some letters lean and others stand up straight or lean backward. Draw light slanted lines through your word: do the letters follow them?

For the grown-up. Left-handed writers tilt the paper the other way (top to the right). Some left-handers write with less slant or almost upright; even slant matters more than the exact angle. See Placing the Paper.

sources.name: A. N. Palmer, The Palmer Method of Business Writing (1915), Lessons 1 to 3: position, posture and pencil hold (public domain; guides on this site)

blocks.html: The first cursive letters all start with an undercurve, the swing up you met in The Basic Cursive Strokes: i, t, u and w.

blocks.name: wr-letter
blocks.cap: Undercurve up, slant line down, undercurve out.

items: i: undercurve up to the middle line, slant down, undercurve out.
t: undercurve up higher, almost to the top line, slant back down, undercurve out.
u: i twice without the dots: up, down, up, down, out.
w: like u, then up once more, ending with a little bridge at the middle line.

blocks.html: Undercurve, slant down, undercurve out. Dot the i and cross the t after the whole word is written.
Waiting to dot and cross keeps the pencil moving through the word. Then you go back once and add every dot and cross.

blocks.title: Write it in cursive
blocks.q: In what order do you write the word it?
steps: Undercurve up to the middle line, slant down, undercurve: that is i without its dot.
Keep going: undercurve up for t, slant down, undercurve out.
Lift the pencil. Dot the i. Cross the t.
blocks.a: Write the whole word, then the dot and the cross.

blocks.name: wr-trace
blocks.cap: Trace it in one go, then the dot and the cross.

blocks.html: Stopping to dot i and cross t in the middle of a word, or making t as tall as l. Check: the top of t stops a little below the top line.
For the grown-up. Palmer teaches i, u and t together; see the guide for small i, u and t. Left-handed writers make the same strokes; the paper tilts the other way.

sources.name: A. N. Palmer, The Palmer Method of Business Writing (1915), Lessons 1 to 3: position, posture and pencil hold (public domain; guides on this site)
Grokipedia, “Cursive”

blocks.html: Loop letters swing up into a loop: e, l, h, k, b and f. The swing up is the undercurve from Cursive i, t, u and w, made taller.

blocks.name: wr-letter
blocks.cap: e has a small loop; l, h, k, b and f have tall loops.

items: e: a small loop that reaches the middle line.
l: a tall loop up to the top line, then slant down and out.
h and k: the loop of l, then a hill (h) or a little loop and kick (k).
b: the loop of l, then up and a little bridge at the middle line.
f: a tall loop on top and a loop below the baseline, closing at the baseline.

blocks.html: Loops are open and leaning: small for e, tall for l, h, k, b and f.
The size of the loop is how a reader tells e from l. A loop pinched shut looks like a slant line; a loop too fat looks like o.

blocks.title: e or l?
blocks.q: How can you make sure your l doesn’t look like an e?
steps: Both are loops.
e stops at the middle line.
l swings all the way up to the top line.
blocks.a: Take the loop of l all the way to the top line.

blocks.name: wr-trace
blocks.cap: Trace cursive l.

blocks.html: Loops that are too fat, closed shut, or the wrong height. Check each loop: open, leaning, and reaching its line.
For the grown-up. Palmer’s small l and the loop letters and small e guides have extra drills.

sources.name: A. N. Palmer, The Palmer Method of Business Writing (1915), Lessons 1 to 3: position, posture and pencil hold (public domain; guides on this site)
Grokipedia, “Cursive”

blocks.html: The c family is a, c, d, g, o and q. Swing up, then curve back around with a downcurve, just as print c does in Circle Letters.

blocks.name: wr-letter
blocks.cap: Swing up, curve back and around, and close the top.

items: a: downcurve around, close at the top, slant down, out.
c: a little hook at the top, then the downcurve.
d: like a, but the line goes up to the top line before coming down.
g and q: like a, with a tail below the baseline (a loop for g).
o: around, close at the top, and out with a little bridge.

blocks.html: Curve back around, then close the top before the line comes down.
A closed top is what makes a an a. An open a looks like u, and an open d looks like c and l (cl).

blocks.title: Read the word
blocks.q: Ben wrote cat, but the top of his a was open. What might a reader see?
steps: An open a looks like u.
So cat could be read as cut.
Closing the a fixes it.
blocks.a: cut instead of cat.

blocks.name: wr-join
blocks.cap: A says cat; B says cut. Look at the tops.

blocks.name: wr-trace
blocks.cap: Trace cursive a.

blocks.html: Leaving the tops of a, d, g and o open. Check each one: did the curve come all the way back up to close?
For the grown-up. See small a and small d, g and q in the Palmer guides.

sources.name: A. N. Palmer, The Palmer Method of Business Writing (1915), Lessons 1 to 3: position, posture and pencil hold (public domain; guides on this site)
Grokipedia, “Cursive”

blocks.html: Hill letters start with an overcurve, a hill: n, m, v, x, y and z. (The other strokes are in The Basic Cursive Strokes.)

blocks.name: wr-letter
blocks.cap: Every one begins over a hill.

items: n: over a hill, slant down, over a second hill, slant down, out.
m: three hills, all the same size.
v: over a hill, slant down, swing up to the middle line, bridge out.
x: over a hill, slant down and out; cross it after the word.
y and z: start over a hill; their tails loop below the baseline.

blocks.html: Hills are round on top. Round hills make n and m; pointed ones would make u and w.
In cursive, n and u are made of the same parts, upside down. The round tops of the hills are what tell them apart.

blocks.title: n or u?
blocks.q: How is cursive n different from cursive u?
steps: n: the tops are round hills and the bottoms are points.
u: the bottoms are round and the tops are points.
So n is round on top, and u is round on the bottom.
blocks.a: n is round on top; u is round on the bottom.

blocks.name: wr-join
blocks.cap: Look for round tops (n, m) and round bottoms (u).

blocks.html: Making the hills pointed, so n looks like u and m looks like w. Check the tops: are they round?
For the grown-up. Palmer teaches the over-motion for m and n early in his course; see the over-motion guide.

sources.name: A. N. Palmer, The Palmer Method of Business Writing (1915), Lessons 1 to 3: position, posture and pencil hold (public domain; guides on this site)
Grokipedia, “Cursive”

blocks.html: Four more letters: r, s, p and j. Cursive r and s look quite different from print, so take them slowly. You will use the loops from Loop Letters and the hills from Hill Letters.

blocks.name: wr-letter
blocks.cap: r and s go up to a point a little above the middle line.

items: r: undercurve up to a point just above the middle line, a tiny step to the right, slant down, out.
s: undercurve up to a point just above the middle line, curve down and back to close at the baseline, out.
p: undercurve, slant down below the baseline, back up, around into a bump, out.
j: undercurve, slant down below the baseline, loop back up, out. Dot it after the word.

blocks.html: r and s peak just above the middle line; p and j go below the baseline.
The print shapes of r and s don’t have a way to join. The cursive shapes start and end on the baseline, so they fit in a word.

blocks.title: r or n?
blocks.q: Mia’s r has a long step on top. What does it look like?
steps: A long step on top looks like a hill.
So r can look like n.
Keep r’s step tiny.
blocks.a: It can look like n; keep the step small.

blocks.name: wr-trace
blocks.cap: Trace cursive s.

blocks.html: Writing print r or s inside a cursive word, or making r’s step so long it looks like n. Check: does the letter start and end on the baseline?
For the grown-up. See small r, small s and small p in the Palmer guides.

sources.name: A. N. Palmer, The Palmer Method of Business Writing (1915), Lessons 1 to 3: position, posture and pencil hold (public domain; guides on this site)
Grokipedia, “Cursive”

blocks.html: Most cursive letters end on the baseline. Four end up high, at the middle line: b, o, v and w. The next letter joins them with a little bridge along the top.

blocks.name: wr-join
blocks.cap: The colored bridges after o, w and b stay up at the middle line.

blocks.html: After b, o, v and w, the join stays up at the middle line, then the next letter begins.
If the join drops to the baseline after o, the next letter starts with an extra swing, and on can look like an. Staying high keeps each word looking like itself.

blocks.title: Write on
blocks.q: How does o join to n?
steps: Make o: around, close at the top.
Go out along the middle line with a little bridge.
From the bridge, go straight into n’s hills.
blocks.a: A bridge at the middle line, then n.

blocks.name: wr-join
blocks.cap: A is on, joined high. B is an. A dropped join makes on look like B.

blocks.html: Dropping down to the baseline after o or w, so on looks like an and we looks like ue. Check: after b, o, v and w, does your pencil stay up?
For the grown-up. These bridges are among the hardest joins in cursive. Short words such as on, we, be, ox, bow and wow make good practice.

sources.name: A. N. Palmer, The Palmer Method of Business Writing (1915), Lessons 1 to 3: position, posture and pencil hold (public domain; guides on this site)
Grokipedia, “Cursive”

blocks.html: Cursive capitals are tall: they reach from the baseline to the top line. The first family, A, C, E and O, starts near the top and curves around to the left, like the c family in The c Family, only bigger.

blocks.name: wr-letter
blocks.cap: All four start near the top and curve left.

items: A: a big oval, closed at the top, then slant down and out.
C: a little curl at the top, then a big curve down and around.
E: a small curve on top, a little loop in the middle, a bigger curve below.
O: a big oval, closed at the top with a small loop.

blocks.html: Start near the top line and curve around to the left. A, C and E join the next letter; O usually doesn’t.
A capital marks the start of a sentence or a name. A full-size cursive capital tells the reader where to begin.

blocks.title: Write the name Ann
blocks.q: How do you write Ann in cursive?
steps: Cursive A: start near the top, curve around, close the top, slant down.
Swing out of A right into the first n.
Then the second n, and an undercurve out.
blocks.a: A joins straight into n n.

blocks.name: wr-trace
blocks.cap: Trace cursive O.

blocks.html: Writing a print capital in a cursive word, or making the capital no taller than a small letter. Check: the capital touches the top line.
For the grown-up. Palmer’s first capitals are A, O and C; see capital A, capital O and capital C.

sources.name: A. N. Palmer, The Palmer Method of Business Writing (1915), Lessons 1 to 3: position, posture and pencil hold (public domain; guides on this site)
Grokipedia, “Palmer Method”

blocks.html: This big family shares a start. M, N, U, V, W, X, Y and Z start with a small hook or a hill near the top, then slant down. H and K start with a slant line from the top.

blocks.name: wr-letter
blocks.cap: Each starts with a little hook, then slants down.

items: M and N: a hook, then hills down: three slants for M, two for N.
U: a hook, slant down, round at the bottom, up, then down again and out.
V: a hook, slant down to a point, then up to the top line.
Y: like U, with a loop tail below the baseline.
H and K: two strokes down from the top; H adds a bar across.

blocks.html: Hook, then slant down. U is round at the bottom and comes back down; V comes to a point and ends at the top.
U and V look alike at the start. Where they end tells them apart: U ends on the baseline and joins; V ends high at the top line.

blocks.title: U or V?
blocks.q: How do you tell cursive U from V?
steps: Look at the bottom: U is round, V is a point.
Look at the end: U comes back down to the baseline.
V goes up and stops at the top line.
blocks.a: U is round and ends low; V is pointed and ends high.

blocks.name: wr-trace
blocks.cap: Trace cursive N.

blocks.html: Leaving off the starting hook of M and N, or mixing up U and V. Check M and N: hook first.
For the grown-up. See capitals M and N and review of Q, U, V, W in the Palmer guides.

sources.name: A. N. Palmer, The Palmer Method of Business Writing (1915), Lessons 1 to 3: position, posture and pencil hold (public domain; guides on this site)
Grokipedia, “Palmer Method”

blocks.html: Next come B, P, R, which start with a slant down and come back up for their bumps, and F and T, which start with a wavy top. (The first capitals are in Cursive Capitals A, C, E and O.)

blocks.name: wr-letter
blocks.cap: B, P and R: slant first, then bumps. T: the wavy top comes first.

items: P: slant down; go back to the top and make one bump that ends at the middle.
B: like P, with a second bump down to the baseline.
R: like P, then a leg that kicks out to the baseline. R joins the next letter.
T: a wavy top, then a stem slanting down and curling left at the bottom.
F: T with a short cross in the middle.

blocks.html: B, P and R: slant, then bumps. F and T: wavy top, then the stem. F has a cross; T doesn’t.
The little cross is the whole difference between cursive F and T, so it needs to be there and be easy to see.

blocks.title: F or T?
blocks.q: Tia wrote her name, but a reader saw Fia. What went wrong?
steps: Cursive T and F share the wavy top and the stem.
F has a cross in the middle; T doesn’t.
A stray mark in the middle of T makes it look like F.
blocks.a: The T had a mark like F’s cross.

blocks.name: wr-trace
blocks.cap: Trace cursive P.

blocks.html: Forgetting the wavy top of F and T, or confusing them. Check: F has a cross; T has none.
For the grown-up. See capital P, capital B and capitals T and F in the Palmer guides. Handwriting books differ a little in these capitals; any clear form is fine.

sources.name: A. N. Palmer, The Palmer Method of Business Writing (1915), Lessons 1 to 3: position, posture and pencil hold (public domain; guides on this site)
Grokipedia, “Palmer Method”

blocks.html: The last seven capitals have shapes of their own: D, G, I, J, L, Q and S. Several look little like print, so they are worth learning well for reading too (the capitals before these).

blocks.name: wr-letter
blocks.cap: I and J start low and swing up. Q looks like a 2.

items: I and J: start at the middle line on the left, swing up to the top, then come down. J keeps going into a loop below the baseline.
L: a little loop at the top, slant down, a little loop on the baseline, out.
S: swing up from the left to a loop at the top, then down and curl back.
Q: a curve at the top, down to the left, a little loop on the baseline: it looks like a 2.
D: slant down, a little loop at the bottom, then a big curve around and up.
G: a tall curve like C that comes back up on the right, then down and out to the next letter. Last, add a little bar at the middle line, the way you cross a t.

blocks.html: I and J swing up from the middle; L and S loop; Q looks like a 2.
These capitals are the ones readers stall on. Knowing them makes cursive notes and names easy to read.

blocks.title: Read a name
blocks.q: A cursive name starts with a letter that looks like a 2. What letter is it?
steps: The cursive capital that looks like a 2 is Q.
So the name starts with Q, like Quinn.
blocks.a: Q

blocks.name: wr-trace
blocks.cap: Trace cursive L.

blocks.html: Not recognizing cursive G, Q, I and J when reading, because they look little like print. Practice reading them as well as writing them.
For the grown-up. Forms of these capitals vary more than most from book to book; teach one clear form and accept others that are readable. Palmer guides: capital I, capital J, capital S, capital G.

sources.name: A. N. Palmer, The Palmer Method of Business Writing (1915), Lessons 1 to 3: position, posture and pencil hold (public domain; guides on this site)
Grokipedia, “Palmer Method”

blocks.html: You have met every cursive letter. Now we join them. Each letter ends with an exit stroke, and that stroke swings right into the next letter’s entry. The pencil stays down until the word is done.

blocks.name: wr-join
blocks.cap: Open dots: where a letter ends. Filled dots: where the next one begins. The colored strokes are the joins.

blocks.html: One letter’s exit becomes the next letter’s entry: write the whole word, then lift and add dots and crosses.
Joined letters are the point of cursive: the hand keeps moving, so writing is smooth and quick, and each word holds together as one shape.

blocks.title: Write cat
blocks.q: How many times do you lift the pencil to write cat in cursive?
steps: c, a and t are joined, so the pencil stays down for the whole word.
Lift once at the end.
Go back and cross the t.
blocks.a: Once, at the end; then cross the t.

blocks.name: wr-join
blocks.cap: A is joined. B is the same letters written apart.

blocks.name: wr-trace
blocks.cap: Trace sun without lifting.

blocks.html: Lifting the pencil after every letter, so the word comes out in pieces. Try saying the whole word as you write it, and keep moving until it’s done.
For the grown-up. Remember the high joins after b, o, v and w from Tricky Connectors. Palmer practices joining with short words such as mum, moon and noon.

sources.name: A. N. Palmer, The Palmer Method of Business Writing (1915), Lessons 1 to 3: position, posture and pencil hold (public domain; guides on this site)
Grokipedia, “Cursive”

blocks.html: Some cursive capitals end on the baseline with an exit stroke, so they join the next letter. Others end high or curl back to the left, so the next letter starts on its own, close by. You learned the capitals in the capitals unit.

blocks.name: wr-join
blocks.cap: A joins n. B ends with a curl, so e starts on its own right after it.

head: Usually join
Usually stand alone
rows: A C E H K M N U
B D O P S V W
and in this style also G J L R Y Z
and in this style also F I Q T X

blocks.html: A capital that ends on the baseline joins; one that ends high or curls back stands alone.
A forced join after a capital that ends up high makes an extra loop the reader has to puzzle out. Starting fresh keeps the word clear.

blocks.title: Write Omar
blocks.q: Does cursive O join the m in Omar?
steps: O ends with a small loop at the top.
That is far from where m begins.
So lift, and start m right next to the O.
blocks.a: No: O stands alone; m starts close by.

blocks.html: Forcing a join after a capital that ends high or on the left. Books and writers differ about a few capitals; either way is fine as long as the name is clear.
For the grown-up. Palmer has a lesson on joining capitals. Names make the best practice: your child’s own name, family names, pets.

sources.name: A. N. Palmer, The Palmer Method of Business Writing (1915), Lessons 1 to 3: position, posture and pencil hold (public domain; guides on this site)

blocks.html: In cursive, the letters of a word join, but words don’t. Finish a word with its exit stroke, lift the pencil, and start the next word a little way over: about the width of a small o.

blocks.name: wr-join
blocks.cap: A is two words. In B, the words are joined into one long word.

blocks.html: Join the letters inside a word; lift and leave a space between words.
The space is the only way a reader can see where one word ends. Joined words look like one long, strange word.

blocks.title: Write a big hat
blocks.q: Where do you lift the pencil in a big hat?
steps: Write a and its exit stroke. Lift.
Leave a small space. Write big, lift, dot the i.
Leave a space. Write hat, lift, cross the t.
blocks.a: After each word.

blocks.name: wr-join
blocks.cap: Three words, each one joined inside.

blocks.html: Joining the last letter of one word to the first letter of the next. Check: can you count the words by the spaces?
For the grown-up. Spacing in cursive works like the finger spaces of print, only a little smaller.

sources.name: A. N. Palmer, The Palmer Method of Business Writing (1915), Lessons 1 to 3: position, posture and pencil hold (public domain; guides on this site)

blocks.html: Now you can write a whole sentence in cursive. Put together what you know: a cursive capital, joined words (capitals and spaces), and an end mark.

blocks.name: wr-join
blocks.cap: A sentence in cursive.

items: Start with a cursive capital.
Join the letters of each word; lift between words.
Dot the i’s and cross the t’s when each word is done.
End with a period, a question mark or an exclamation mark.

blocks.html: Capital, joined words with spaces, dots and crosses, end mark. Steady and readable comes before fast.
A sentence is for a reader. If the letters lose their shapes when you hurry, the reader has to guess.

blocks.title: Check a sentence
blocks.q: Leo wrote: we can swim, in cursive. What two things are missing?
steps: A sentence starts with a capital: We.
A sentence ends with a mark: a period.
Fixed: We can swim.
blocks.a: The capital W and the period.

blocks.name: wr-trace
blocks.cap: Trace I can: two words, a lift between them.

opts.title: My cursive sentence
items: A cursive capital at the start
Letters joined inside each word
A space between words
Dots and crosses added
An end mark

blocks.html: Speeding up until the letters lose their shapes. Slow down: neat first, quick later.
For the grown-up. Palmer’s course ends with sentences and names; see line-writing. One sentence a day, copied carefully, is plenty.

sources.name: A. N. Palmer, The Palmer Method of Business Writing (1915), Lessons 1 to 3: position, posture and pencil hold (public domain; guides on this site)

blocks.html: Good writers read their own writing. After a sentence, check the shapes of your letters, not just the spelling (Writing Sentences in Cursive).

head: Check
Letters
If not, it looks like
rows: e l b h k f
e → i, l → a slant line

blocks.name: wr-join
blocks.cap: Letter 3 floats above the baseline.

blocks.html: Check tops, loops, hills, heights and slant, one letter at a time.
One badly shaped letter can change a word: clear can be read as dear if c and l run together into d.

blocks.title: Spot the letter
blocks.q: In Ava’s word little, the first l is no taller than e. What could a reader see?
steps: A short l with a small loop looks like e.
So little could read as eittle.
Make the l reach the top line.
blocks.a: The l looks like e.

blocks.name: hand-slant
blocks.cap: Letter 3, an l, stands up straight while the others lean.

blocks.html: Checking spelling but not shapes. Read your word as if someone else wrote it: could any letter be read as another?
For the grown-up. Choose one thing to check per day (tops one day, loops the next). That is easier than looking for everything at once.

sources.name: A. N. Palmer, The Palmer Method of Business Writing (1915), Lessons 1 to 3: position, posture and pencil hold (public domain; guides on this site)

blocks.html: A signature is your name written in your own handwriting. Many people sign in cursive. You can sign a card, a letter, a drawing you made, or a library card.

blocks.name: wr-join
blocks.cap: A clear signature: a capital for each name, letters joined, a space between.

blocks.html: Write your name the same way each time, and keep it readable.
A signature shows that you wrote or agreed to something. Signing the same way every time makes it yours, and a readable one lets people know who signed.

blocks.title: Practice a signature
blocks.q: How can Omar practice his signature?
steps: Write his first name in cursive, with a cursive capital O.
Leave a space and write his last name the same way.
Write it five times, the same each time.
blocks.a: Neat cursive, the same way every time.

blocks.name: wr-trace
blocks.cap: Trace a short first name.

blocks.html: Thinking a signature must be fancy or impossible to read. A clear, steady signature is a good one.
For the grown-up. Some children like to practice their signature on cards and notes they send. Grown-ups sign forms, checks and letters the same way.

blocks.html: Writing cursive and reading it are two skills. Most cursive letters look like their print letters, but a few look quite different. Learn these well (the last capitals).

blocks.name: wr-letter
blocks.cap: Cursive r, s, z, G, I, J and Q: the letters readers stall on most.

head: Cursive
Hint
rows: a point with a tiny step on top
a point that curves down and closes
a hill, then a loop below like a tail
a tall curve like C with a short part on the right
start at the middle line on the left and swing up; J has a loop below

blocks.html: Match each cursive letter to its print letter; give the odd ones extra practice.
Notes, cards and old letters are often in cursive. Reading every letter quickly means you can read them all.

blocks.title: Match the letter
blocks.q: A cursive capital starts low on the left, swings up to the top line, and comes down with a loop below the baseline. Which letter is it?
steps: I and J both start low and swing up.
Only J has a loop below the baseline.
blocks.a: J

blocks.name: wr-sort
blocks.cap: Which cursive letters look like their print letters?

blocks.html: Stalling on cursive capitals that look little like print. Practice reading them on their own, then in names.
For the grown-up. A quick game: write a cursive letter and let your child name it. Mix in the hard ones often.

sources.name: Grokipedia, “Cursive”
A. N. Palmer, The Palmer Method of Business Writing (1915), Lessons 1 to 3: position, posture and pencil hold (public domain; guides on this site)

blocks.html: To read a cursive word, read it letter by letter at first, then as a whole. You know the letters from Reading Cursive Letters and the joins from Joining Letters.

blocks.name: wr-join
blocks.cap: Can you read it?

items: Find the start of each letter. Joins come between letters, so look for the slant lines.
Watch the high joins after b, o, v and w: the next letter starts up at the middle line.
Say the sounds, then the word. Does it make sense in the sentence?

blocks.html: Read each letter, check the tricky joins, then read the whole word and see if it makes sense.
Guessing from the first letter leads to mistakes: brown could be read as brain. Checking each letter gets it right.

blocks.title: Read it
blocks.q: The picture above shows two words. What are they?
steps: The first word: b, r, o, w, n. The join after o stays high.
The second word: b, e, a, r.
Together: brown bear.
blocks.a: brown bear

blocks.html: Guessing a word from its first letter. Read every letter, especially after b, o, v and w, then check that the word makes sense.
For the grown-up. Short notes in cursive (a lunch-box note, a grocery list) make good daily reading practice.

sources.name: Grokipedia, “Cursive”

blocks.html: Old letters and documents were handwritten in the styles of their time. With cursive, you can read many of them. Here are two things to know first (Reading Cursive Words).

Until about 200 years ago, a lowercase s was often written as a tall long s: ſ. It looks much like f, but it has no crossbar, or only a little nub on the left side. It was used at the start or in the middle of a word, and the short s at the end. So Congress was written Congreſs. The heading of the Bill of Rights at the National Archives has exactly this word.
In old writing, a tall s that looks like f is the long s. Read it as s.
Knowing the long s turns a strange word like Congrefs into the word it is: Congress.

The Declaration of Independence was written out on parchment in 1776 by Timothy Matlack, in a careful style called English round hand. Its title line reads “The unanimous Declaration of the thirteen united States of America.” Writers then used capitals more freely than we do: States has a capital, but united doesn’t.

blocks.title: Read the word
blocks.q: How do you read ſiſter?
steps: The first letter is a long s: read it as s.
The third letter is also a long s.
So the word is sister.
blocks.a: sister

blocks.name: wr-sort

cards.text: the s in the middle of first

cards.why: At the end of a word, the short s was used.

cards.text: the s at the end of is

blocks.cap: Which s would an old writer use?

blocks.html: Reading the long s as f, so Congreſs becomes Congrefs. Look for the crossbar: f has one all the way through; the long s doesn’t.

For the grown-up. The National Archives shows the Declaration, the Constitution and the Bill of Rights online. Reading a line or two of an old document together, with its transcript beside it, is a good way to practice.
